claims.text: The AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles were synthesized by pulsed laser deposition on a silicon nitride membrane.
The AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles are initially FCC.
The initial nanoparticles may have elliptical, icosahedral, or truncated-octahedral shapes.
Surface-energy minimization drives Au and Cu segregation to the nanoparticle surface.
Segregation in sub-5 nm AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles is not limited by sluggish bulk diffusion.
High configurational entropy stabilizes the FCC bulk structure.
For sub-5 nm particles, surface-energy terms dominate the Gibbs free energy because of the high surface-to-volume ratio.
Au and Cu have lower surface energies than the other components of the alloy.
Surface enrichment in Au and Cu lowers the total energy of the nanoparticles.
Surface-segregated Au and Cu subsequently evaporate.
Au and Cu evaporate because their boiling points are relatively low compared with Pt.
The surface-driven mechanism becomes dominant at approximately 600–800 K.
At 600–800 K, a surface-diffusion activation barrier is overcome, enabling rapid segregation and evaporation.
Icosahedral particles have higher-surface-energy facets and therefore segregate and evaporate faster than truncated-octahedral particles.
Heating causes a progressive loss of sub-5 nm particles.
Heating widens the nanoparticle size distribution.
Heating reshapes elliptical nanoparticles into spherical particles.
The bulk remains FCC while the nanoparticle composition changes during heating.
The surface-driven mechanism is dominant for particles smaller than 10 nm.
For larger particles, sluggish bulk diffusion may dominate over surface-energy effects.

contradictions.description: The falsification experiment asks whether surface-energy gradients alone explain phase separation, whereas the stated mechanism additionally requires activated surface diffusion and element-specific volatility or boiling-point differences. Suppressing only bulk diffusion therefore does not isolate a surface-energy-only explanation.
